 1                                  I. INTRODUCTION

 2   Q   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A   Michael P. Gorman. My business address is 16690 Swingley Ridge Road, Suite 140,

 4       Chesterfield, MO 63017.



 5   Q   WHAT IS YOUR OCCUPATION?

 6   A   I am an expert consultant in the field of public utility regulation and a Managing Principal

 7       and President of the firm Brubaker & Associates, Inc. (“BAI”), energy, economic and

 8       regulatory consultants.



 9   Q   PLEASE       DESCRIBE        YOUR       EDUCATIONAL            AND      PROFESSIONAL

10       BACKGROUND.

11   A   This information is included as Appendix A to my testimony.



12   Q   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU APPEARING IN THIS PROCEEDING?

13   A   I am appearing on behalf of the Federal Executive Agencies (“FEA”) and Louisiana Energy

14       Services, L.L.C. d/b/a URENCO USA (“LES”). FEA and LES operate facilities in the

15       Southwestern Public Service Company’s (“SPS” or “Company”) service territory.

16   Q   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY IN THIS PROCEEDING?




                                            Page 1
                              Direct Testimony of Michael P. Gorman
                                NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1   A   I will respond to the Company’s proposed rate design for the Large General Service

 2       Transmission (“LGS-T”) Rate Class in its proposed pilot program for a time-of-use

 3       fuel pilot for LGS-T rate class.

 4              For the reasons outlined below, I oppose the Company’s proposed

 5       adjustment to the LGS-T rate design based on the following:

 6          •   The Company’s proposal to adjust the ratchet demand in units from 60%
 7              ratchet over the last 11 months, to an 85% ratchet is not consistent with cost
 8              causation and should not be approved. The Company’s existing LGS-T rate
 9              design is more aligned with cost-causation and is fair and reasonable.

10          •   If the Company’s proposed LGS-T demand ratchet is approved, contrary to
11              my recommendation, the Commission should make a greater movement to
12              the cost of service for the LGS-T rate class to mitigate the economic harm
13              to customers that are allocated a disproportionate share of production and
14              transmission costs caused by the LGS-T rate design change, which is not
15              consistent with how these costs are allocated across jurisdiction and across
16              New Mexico rate classes.

17          •   The Company’s proposal to discontinue a power factor credit for customers
18              with a leading power factor over 0.95 is imbalanced with its power factor
19              penalty position and should be rejected.

20          •   The Company’s proposed change in the power supply credits for the Salt
21              Lake City Area Integrated Projects (“SLCA Integrated Projects”) supply
22              should be aligned with the increase in production and transmission capacity
23              costs.

24          •   The increase in production and transmission capacity credit for the
25              Renewable*Connect (“R*C”) supply should align with the increase in
26              production demand costs included in the LGS-T rates.

27          •   The administrative charge included in the R*C Rider should exclude SPS
28              administrative costs that are recovered in the tariff base rates. Only
29              incremental administrative cost, if any, should be included in the
30              development of R*C Rider charges.

                                            Page 2
                                Direct Testimony of Michael P. Gorman
                                  NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT




 1             •   SPS’s proposal to recover Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”) deficiency
 2                 payments through the Fuel and Purchased Power Cost Adjustment Clause
 3                 (“FPPCAC”) should be denied. The Company seeks to recover a $4.93
 4                 million SPP penalty for the December 1, 2026 through March 31, 2027
 5                 period from New Mexico customers. This penalty has not been proven to
 6                 be prudent and should be removed from SPS cost of service.



 7                       II. LARGE GENERAL SERVICE
 8                    TRANSMISSION (“LGS-T”) RATE DESIGN

 9   Q   IS SPS PROPOSING CHANGES IN THE DESIGN OF ITS LGS-T RATE?

10   A   Yes. SPS witness Alexander Trowbridge is proposing five changes in the LGS-T

11       rate design:

12             1) Change the minimum demand billing. He proposes to change the demand
13                billing ratchet from 60% to 85%. This changes the monthly billing demand
14                unit from a) the higher of the current month metered demand or 60% of the
15                highest demand billing unit metered over the last 11 months, to b) the higher
16                of the current month metered demand or 85% of the highest demand billing
17                unit metered over the last 11 months. This increases the demand billing
18                units for the 69 kV and 115 kV customers by 5.4%/3.6%, and 2.5%/2.6%
19                in summer/winter periods, respectively. Mr. Trowbridge estimates that the
20                increase in billing demand units is offset by a reduction in the demand
21                charge by about 2.5%.1

22             2) A reduction to the LGS-T non-fuel energy rate from $0.006205/.kWh to
23                $0.00149/kWh for the 115 kV service, and shift the non-fuel cost recovery
24                to an increased demand charge cost recovery. This shifts over $37 million
25                of LGS-T cost of service from non-fuel cost recovery to demand charge cost
26                recovery for 115 kV customers.

27             3) He is proposing to increase the Kilovolt-Ampere Reactive (“kVAR”)
28                charge, or Power Factor (“PF”) penalty, for LGS-T customers to a lagging

         1
             Direct Testimony of Alexander G. Trowbridge ("Trowbridge Direct") at 50.

                                               Page 3

 1                  PF of 0.95 from the 0.90 PF, and eliminate the leading power factor credit.
 2                  This increases the power factor penalty charges in the 115 kV LGS-T rate
 3                  by over $4 million per year.2

 4              4) The Company's proof of revenue is based on adjustments to
 5                 Renewable*Connect credits that do not align with changes in LGS-T
 6                 production demand cost. The Renewable*Connect production credit should
 7                 align with SPS test year changes in fixed production costs.

 8              5) The Cannon Air Force Base (“AFB”) credit for hydro delivery capacity
 9                 payment should be adjusted to align with SPS increased test year production
10                 and transmission capacity costs.



11   Q      PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR RESPONSE TO SPS’S PROPOSED RATE

12          DESIGN CHANGES TO THE LGS-T RATE.

13   A      My recommendations and response to SPS’s proposed revision to the Rate LGS-T

14          are as follows:

15              1) The Company’s proposal to change the rate to an 85% demand ratchet from
16                 a 60% demand ratchet does not align with how Production and
17                 Transmission (“P&T”) capacity costs are allocated across the SPS total
18                 system, nor does it align with P&T capacity cost allocation within the New
19                 Mexico retail system. P&T capacity costs are allocated based on a 12
20                 Coincident Peak (“12 CP”) across jurisdictions3 and are allocated using an
21                 Average and Excess 4 CP (“A&E 4CP”) methodology within the New
22                 Mexico retail jurisdiction. The A&E 4 CP allocators are based on base
23                 demand and demands in excess of base demand. SPS’s P&T capacity costs
24                 are not allocated based on demands that are within 85% of the system or
25                 class peak demand. Therefore, the proposed 85% ratchet demand for the
26                 LGS-T class does not align with cost causation, and should not be approved.

 1             2) If the LGS-T rate design proposed by the Company is approved, then the
 2                allocation of the revenue deficiency across rate classes should be aligned
 3                with the cost of service, and the LGS-T rate class should receive a below
 4                system average increase. This will mitigate the harm to customers within
 5                the LGS-T rate class that are being asked to pay a disproportionate share of
 6                P&T demand cost.

 7             3) The Renewable*Connect credit at proposed rates does not reflect the
 8                Company’s proposed increase in LGS-T production demand cost. The
 9                Renewable*Connect credit should reflect production capacity cost
10                avoidance and should be adjusted to align with the proposed test year
11                production demand cost increase.

12             4) The SLCA Integrated Projects credits also do not follow the increase in
13                SPS’ test year P&T demand costs. The SLCA delivers hydro capacity to
14                SPS and provides SPS with delivered production capacity and energy to its
15                control area. The SLCA credit proposed by SPS should be rejected, and an
16                adjustment to this credit that reflects the change in test year P&T capacity
17                cost should be approved.



18   II.A. LGS-T RATE DEMAND RACHET

19   Q   DESCRIBE WHY SPS IS PROPOSING TO CHANGE THE DEMAND

20       RACHET IN THE LGS-T RATE CLASS, FROM 60% IN THE CURRENT

21       RATE TO 85% UNDER THE PROPOSED REDESIGNED LGS-T RATE .

22   A   SPS Witness Trowbridge states that this billing demand rachet aligns with cost-

23       causation, promotes equity and stability in revenue recovery, and enhances SPS’s

24       cost-recovery alignment across the growing class.4




         4
             Trowbridge Direct at 49.

                                               Page 5
                                Direct Testimony of Michael P. Gorman
                                  NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1                  In forming his recommendation, Mr. Trowbridge states that the Company

 2       looked at five years of the LGS-T class billing demands for the LGS-T rate class

 3       and chose an 85% ratchet to strike a balance between protecting the utility revenue

 4       requirements and avoiding undue cross-subsidization. However, he provided no

 5       evidence that changing the LGS-T rate demand ratchet from 60% to 85% aligns

 6       with SPS’s cost to serve the LGS-T rate class, nor does it align with cost causation.5

 7       Consequently, his finding that the proposed change to the LGS-T billing demand

 8       ratchet will avoid undue cost subsidization is without merit.



 9   Q   DO YOU AGREE WITH SPS WITNESS TROWBRIDGE THAT HIS

10       PROPOSED ADJUSTMENT TO THE LGS-T RATE TO REFLECT AN 85%

11       DEMAND RATCHET ALIGNS WITH CAUSATION?

12   A   No. The proposed change does not align with cost causation. The allocation of

13       demand costs within the LGS-T class should align with how SPS allocates its P&T

14       demand cost to the LGS-T rate class. Mr. Trowbridge’s proposed 85% demand

15       ratchet does not align with how demand costs are allocated to the LGS-T class.

16                  Mr. Trowbridge proposes to allocate demand costs within the LGS-T rate

17       class based on demands being no less than 85% of their annual peak billing demand.

18       However, the allocation of P&T capacity costs across the SPS total company

 1   system and retail classes in New Mexico is not based on demands within 85% of

 3             Rather, SPS allocates its P&T capacity across its jurisdictions based on the

 4   use of a 12 CP cost allocator.6 A 12 CP demand allocator does not allocate demands

 5   based on only monthly demands that are at least 85% of the annual peak demand.

 6   In allocating P&T capacity costs across rate classes within the New Mexico

 7   jurisdiction, SPS uses an A&E 4 CP allocator. The A&E 4 CP allocator assigns

 9   Again, this P&T demand cost allocator is not designed to allocate demand cost

11   peak demand.

12             Mr. Trowbridge’s proposed 85% demand ratchet for the LGS-T class does

13   not align with how P&T demand costs are allocated across the SPS total Company,

14   nor is it aligned with how the P&T capacity costs are allocated to the LGS-T rate

15   class. Therefore, his proposed change in the LGS-T demand ratchet to 85% from

16   60% does not follow cost-of-service nor cost causation. Mr. Trowbridge’s proposal

17   to change the LGS-T rate demand ratchet to 85% from 60% should be rejected.

 1   Q.     IF THE COMMISSION APPROVES THE REDESIGN OF THE LGS-T

 2          RATE, SHOULD THE COMMISSION MITIGATE THE IMPACT ON

 3          CERTAIN CUSTOMERS WITHIN THE CLASS THAT IS HARMED BY

 4          THE RATE REDESIGN?

 5   A      Yes. SPS’s proposed redesign of the LGS-T rate class will allocate P&T costs

 6          within the LGS-T class differently than how those costs are allocated across the

 7          total SPS system and across retail customer classes in New Mexico. Using a peak

 8          demand class allocation would reduce the P&T capacity cost allocated to the LGS-

 9          T rate class, which would mitigate the impact on certain customers in this class

10          harmed by the rate design. About one-third of the customers within the LGS-T rate

11          class will unjustifiably pick up an increased share of the P&T demand cost allocated

12          to this rate class.7 Increasing the P&T demand cost to a third of the class is in

13          addition to the over-allocation of P&T costs to the LGS-T rate class via the gradual

14          movement to cost of service across all retail rate classes. Under the Company’s

15          proposed class revenue allocation, the LGS-T rate class is being allocated an

16          increase above its cost of service in an effort to moderate the impact on other rate

17          classes that are priced below cost of service.8 The use of a gradual movement to

18          the cost of service mitigates the effects of harmful rate increases to certain

 3   To mitigate the impact on certain LGS-T customers caused by the proposed

 5      1) The increase to the LGS-T rate class should be as close to the cost of service

 1                 III. LGS-T POWER FACTOR ADJUSTMENT

 2   Q   IS THE COMPANY PROPOSING TO CHANGE THE POWER FACTOR

 3       REVISION OF THE LGS-T RATE CLASSES PROCEEDING?

 4   A   Yes. Mr. Trowbridge proposes an increase of the Power Factor ("PF") charge for

 5       the LGS-T rate class for customers based on a 95% lagging PF target rather than

 6       the 90% lagging PF target. This change increases the kVAR charges for customers

 7       with PF below 95%. He proposes to increase the PF excess kVAR charge from

 8       0.77/kVAR to 7.57/kVAR, for delivered kVARs that are more than 0.33 of metered

 9       KW. He also proposes to eliminate PF credit for customers who have a leading PF

10       in excess of 0.95.



11   Q   WHAT IS PF AND HOW DOES IT IMPACT SPS’S POWER SUPPLY

12       COSTS?

13   A   Power Factor represents the efficiency in which power demands on the system are

14       met and SPS cost to serve those demands. At the utility generator, power is

15       generated in apparent power, measured in “kVA,” which equates to the amount of

16       real power generated, measured in “kW,” and reactive power generated, measured

17       in “kVAR.” A majority of electrical applications require real power (kW) to

18       operate. However, certain types of inductive load, for example motors, consume

19       both kW and kVAR. At a 1.0 PF, the system is regarded as most efficient because


                                            Page 10
                          Direct Testimony of Michael P. Gorman
                            NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1   all kVA generated can be consumed as real power, kW. As the PF moves below

 2   one, the generator must produce more kVAs in order to serve customers’ real

 3   power, kW, demands. This can increase the utility’s cost of serving its customers’

 4   real power demands, kW.

 5          The SPP Open Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”) requires participants

 6   to maintain a system PF in the range of 0.95 lagging to a 0.95 leading PF. A leading

 7   PF can offset a lagging PF and help keep the system PF within the specified

 8   tolerance range. For PFs below the targeted level, or 0.95, SPS incurs additional

 9   costs to keep its system PF within the targeted range.

10          To recognize this power supply cost for SPS, it imposes a PF penalty charge

11   on customers that have PFs below 0.90 under current rates, or under 0.95 under the

12   Company's proposed tariff rates. These PF penalties allow customers to either

13   choose between paying increased power supply cost if they have low PF load, or

14   the customer can elect to install PF correction equipment and improve its PF,

15   avoiding the higher power supply costs.         PF correction equipment includes

16   installing capacitors or other equipment at the point of delivery, which can alter the

17   PF of the customer’s load.




                                        Page 11
                                Direct Testimony of Michael P. Gorman
                                  NMPRC Docket No. 25-00079-UT


 1   Q     DOES SPS HAVE TO COMPLY WITH PF RANGES IN MAINTAINING

 2         ITS POWER SUPPLY WITHIN THE SPP?

 3   A     Yes. SPP’s OATT specifies that SPS is required to maintain a power factor range

 4         of 0.95 lagging to 0.95 leading.9



 5   Q     IS MR. TROWBRIDGE’S PROPOSED DEVELOPMENT OF THE POWER

 6         FACTOR         PENALTY         FOR        LAGGING           POWER       FACTORS

 7         REASONABLE?

 8   A      Yes. The PF targets appear to comply with the SPP OATT system targets and

 9         align with SPS's cost to maintain SPS’s system PF within the SPP targeted PF

10         range.



11   Q     IS MR. TROWBRIDGE PROPOSING TO ELIMINATE THE LEADING PF

12         CREDIT ABOVE 0.95 PF?

13   A     Yes. He states that the current PF credit for leading power factors greater than 0.95

14         can be eliminated because PF issues are inherently localized and do not provide

15         system-wide offsets. He opines that a customer with an excellent PF at one location

16         does not mitigate the burdens caused by a poor PF in another location. Hence, he

 1       maintains that a leading PF credit simply results in subsidies to certain customers

 2       without any benefits to the system.10



 3   Q   DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. TROWBRIDGE’S PROPOSAL TO

 4       ELIMINATE PF CREDITS OR POWER FACTOR IN EXCESS OF 0.95?

 5   A   No. Customers with leading PFs above 95% can offset the lagging PF caused by

 6       other customers. Mr. Trowbridge claimed that if the Company pays a leading PF

 7       credit, it is not receiving benefits because the leading PF may not reduce SPS’s

 8       costs. However, this same rationale can be used to oppose his recommended

 9       lagging PF penalty charge. That is, customers with a lagging PF below 95% may

10       not result in a system PF outside of the SPP tolerance range and SPS may not incur

11       a PF charge caused by a customer with a PF below 0.95. Hence, charging customers

12       a PF penalty for PF below 0.95 may impose costs on the customers that are not

13       based on costs incurred by SPS. That is, load diversity within the system may offset

14       a PF cost caused by specific customers.

15                 I recommend the same PF credit be imposed on customers with leading PF

16       in excess of 0.95 to balance the Company’s proposed penalty charge for customers

17       with lagging PF below 0.95.
